function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands on your machine or push changes to a remote repository, but I can walk you through the entire workflow step‑by‑step so you can finish it yourself.  
Below is a **complete guide** that covers:

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 1 | Clone the repo | Get the source code locally |
| 2 | Analyse the repo | Understand the app’s structure & dependencies |
| 3 | Create Dockerfile | Package the app into a container |
| 4 | Create Kubernetes YAMLs | Deploy the container to a cluster |
| 5 | Create GitHub Actions workflow | Automate CI/CD on pushes |
| 6 | Commit & push | Persist the changes |

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use HTTPS instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo

Open the repo in your favourite editor (VS Code, Vim, etc.) and look for:

| File | What to look for | Why it matters |
|------|------------------|----------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies, scripts, start command | Determines runtime & build steps |
| `app.js` / `index.js` | Entry point | Dockerfile entrypoint |
| `README.md` | Port number, environment variables | Helps set `EXPOSE` & service ports |
| `.env.example` | Config vars | May need to be passed to Docker/K8s |

### Quick Summary (example)

Assuming the repo contains:

- `app.js` that listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`
- `package.json` with `"start": "node app.js"`
- No Dockerfile or K8s manifests

---

## 3️⃣ Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> - Uses a lightweight Alpine image.  
> - Installs only production deps (`npm ci`).  
> - Exposes port 3000 (default for many Node apps).  
> - Uses the existing `npm start` script.

---

## 4️⃣ Create Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` and inside it two files: `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.

### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "128Mi"
```

### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Why these files?**  
> - Deployment scales to 2 replicas.  
> - Service exposes the app on port 80 via a LoadBalancer (adjust as per your cluster).  
> - Environment variable `PORT` ensures the container listens on the correct port.

---

## 5️⃣ Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want to auto‑deploy
```

> **What this does**  
> - Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> - Builds the Docker image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> - You can extend it to deploy to a cluster if you wish.

---

## 6️⃣ Commit & Push the Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/ .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re using a fork**  
> Push to your fork and then open a Pull Request against the original repo.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A Dockerfile that builds a container image.  
- Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs ready for `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.  
- A GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds & pushes the image on every push to `main`.  

Feel free to tweak the images, resource limits, or deployment strategy to fit your environment. Happy coding!
